summary: Lists extra requirements for address selection mechanisms that work with the default rules in RFC 3484, to solve problems seen in environments with multiple prefixes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a computer has more than one address, it must choose well. This paper lists what a better choosing system needs.

questions: how to improve default address selection
how should address selection work with multiple networks
what security risks does address selection have
subtitle: What address selection mechanisms must support to work reliably

tldr.problem: RFC 3484 defines default address selection rules for IPv6, but these default rules fail in environments where hosts have multiple addresses or address prefixes. Networks need better automatic address selection.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists eleven requirements for address selection mechanisms that can work alongside or extend RFC 3484 to handle multi-prefix and multi-address scenarios automatically, including support for dynamic updates, multiple interfaces, and security.
tldr.outcome: Subsequent RFCs (particularly RFC 6724) built improved address selection algorithms that implement these requirements, enabling more reliable multi-address deployment.

today: RFC 5221 is Informational. It was followed by RFC 6724, which updates RFC 3484 with improved address selection rules that address many of these requirements. Address selection remains an ongoing concern in IPv6 networks with multiple prefixes or providers.

sections.title: The Address Selection Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3484 specifies a default algorithm for choosing between multiple source and destination addresses in IPv6. However, the algorithm does not always choose correctly in real network environments, particularly when a host has multiple address prefixes or belongs to multiple subnets.

The problems are compounded because configuring RFC 3484's rules is complex and requires users or administrators to understand their network topology, which many lack the knowledge to do. This document identifies the requirements for an automated mechanism that extends or improves upon RFC 3484, so hosts can select addresses correctly without manual configuration.
sections.eli5: Right now, computers use a simple rule to pick addresses. That rule does not always work when a computer has many addresses. We need a system that learns the rules automatically instead of making people configure them by hand.

sections.title: Eleven Core Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies eleven requirements any address selection mechanism must meet. The mechanism must be effective—capable of actually modifying address selection behavior to solve the problematic cases described in RFC 5220. It must support appropriate timing, allowing nodes to obtain selection information when they need it without degrading usability or imposing long processing delays.

The mechanism must support dynamic behavior updates, so administrators can change address selection rules when network structures change. It must handle node-specific behavior, allowing different nodes on the same subnet to behave differently based on their assigned prefixes. It must also support application-specific behavior, working alongside application-layer address selection APIs when needed.

Additional requirements include support for multiple interfaces, central control by administrators or service providers, next-hop selection coordination with routing mechanisms, and backward compatibility with existing RFC 3493 socket interfaces, RFC 3484 address selection, and existing security expectations.
sections.eli5: A good address selection system needs to solve real problems, work fast, change when networks change, let administrators control it, work with many network cards, and not break old programs.

sections.title: Security Threats and Protections
sections.content:
Deploying an automated address selection mechanism introduces security risks. The RFC identifies three classes of threats: leakage (malicious nodes collecting policy information and leaking it), hijacking (attackers injecting malicious policy information to redirect traffic), and denial of service (flooding a policy controller to prevent delivery of correct selection rules).

To counter these threats, the mechanism must provide integrity protection for both the policy information and the messages carrying it. It must also provide authentication and authorization of parties involved in the protocol. The RFC recommends using existing protocols like IPsec rather than inventing new security mechanisms. These security services are critical because address selection policy directly affects which servers a host connects to, making it a valuable target for attackers.
sections.eli5: Bad actors could try to trick a computer into sending data to the wrong place by lying about address rules. The system needs to check that rules come from a trusted source and cannot be changed in transit.

sections.title: Multi-Prefix Scenarios
sections.content:
The underlying problem this RFC addresses is that IPv6 networks increasingly have multiple prefixes due to multi-homing, site changes, and transitions from IPv4. A single host may have addresses from different prefixes or providers simultaneously. Selecting the correct source address depends on the destination address, the network topology, and policy—not just on a simple default rule.

In some cases, a node may be connected to multiple subnets with different prefixes, each with specific routing paths. In others, a node may receive multiple prefixes from the same provider or transition between prefixes during network renumbering. Without a mechanism to dynamically learn and apply correct selection rules, hosts either fail to communicate or connect to the wrong endpoints.
sections.eli5: In the real world, networks are messy. A computer might be in two places at once (with two different addresses), or move to a new network. The old rules for picking an address do not handle this well.

sections.title: Deployment and Management
sections.content:
Effective address selection is essential for IPv6 deployment in complex networks. Manual configuration is not scalable for large organizations or consumer networks. An automated mechanism that satisfies these requirements enables seamless multi-address support without requiring users to understand network topology.

The document emphasizes that any solution must work in both managed networks (where administrators can configure policies) and unmanaged networks (where policies must be distributed automatically). It must accommodate single-interface hosts as well as multi-homed systems. The mechanism should integrate with existing management infrastructure and work compatibly with other protocol mechanisms like DNS, DHCP, and routing protocols.
sections.eli5: Network administrators need a way to tell all computers how to pick addresses without manually configuring each one. The system should also work for people at home who do not have IT support.

items.title: Effectiveness
items.text: Solve the problems RFC 3484 does not handle.

items.title: Timing
items.text: Let nodes learn rules when needed without delay.

items.title: Dynamic Updates
items.text: Allow rule changes when networks change.

items.title: Node-Specific Behavior
items.text: Support different rules for different hosts.

items.title: Central Control
items.text: Let admins manage address selection policy.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: Work with RFC 3484 and existing applications.
